pages.transcription:
March 31, Hotel Wyndham 42 West 58 Street
Dear Hannah and Manfred, we got your letter about Eva and I was very
ashamed. I should have foreseen that our first news about Salmon would
have frightened you as you have perhaps supposed that we did hide you dread-
ful things - we had written in whole sincerity with the feeling that it was
a trifling misunderstanding between Mr. Salmon's goodhearted vanity and her
Manfredish incapability of showing her feelings. But imagine our situation -
should we have invented some story or told you the whole truth as it was and
a simple and innocent ~~true~~ truth? Altogether we are satisfied it came as
it came. We have an excellent impression of Mrs. Schaeffer, her reports are so
clear and human and we have the best feeling that the surroundings are excellent
for Eva. She will come to New York now in her schoolholidays and we shall have
her with us for a few days and she will do all to multiply her acquaintances
that you may be still more sure. Dont believe that I am severe; I know that
this incapacity of showing her feelings is a heritage and who has more ex-
perience in dealing with it than we both, you with Manfred and I with Lotte.
But on the other hand I think it is useful if a certain carelessness in
exterior details is corrected just in these decisive years of formation and
I believe that the example of Schaeffers will be an excellent one. My
dear Hannah, you cannot imagine how we are disqusted of the impoliteness
the rudeness, the arrogant way of the American children and it is an enor-
mous advantage that she will brought up in our conceptions; on the other
hand it will {in the coming world} be necessary to be effective, reliable and
independent, it will not be a world for dreamers and the earlier she
learns that one has to think for oneself, the better for her. That's why I insist
that in the small matters like letter-writing she has not always to be remin-
ded and that her feeling for responsability must get independent as soon
as possible. More and more I see, that one has to do all one self and that
not as in our own youth one had a large and influential family around
to smoothe the ways; life also after the war will ask much more energy
than was asked from our generation. Please rely upon us and dont be
frightened that your poor lamb has to suffer here; I know it is a hard strain
for you both to miss her and I understand that in certain hours you will
even regret having sent her away. But we have all to overcome this ordeal
- also our life is disturbed here by the constant uncertainty. I am dis-
gusted to go from one place to the other and to decide always and without

pages.transcription:
to come to an definite decision. I suppose we will go back to Rio for the
summer as we could not stay here in New York in the summer; the great diffi-
culty is how to assure the in advance how to come back when the summer
begins as visitors-visa will be not available (especially in case of declaration
of open war) on the other hand if we would take an immigrants visa it could
easely be misunderstood as if I would like to change my citizenship. You cannot
imagine how many of such questions assail me every day and in the same time
the dirty letters and cables for affidavits and visas. But I continue working,
my book on Brasil (which will be perhaps useful to tighten the cultural rela-
tions between the English-speaking and Latin world) will appear here in English
in autumn (the translator is frightfully slow) and I have some new work
on hand; so we have no material worries, but the moral ones are big enough.
The United States will give England all possible help, the whole country
is transformed in an enormous factory. What we are afraid of personally is
to become cut off during the duration of war and also for Eva we would
not like that, as nobody can foresee how long this will take.
I shall see today or tomorrow Edemanns brother. We have a few good
friends here and have to avoid the big crowd of the refugees. I have made
no public appearance and do not write for newspapers, because the most
important is for me to continue my work quietly and to keep fit. Lotte feels
much better since we left Petropolis; the winter was hard and endless, in
more of six weeks we had not a single walk there. About my other more
material things I shall write to Mr. Wilmot in the next days and send
you a copy of the letter so that you may be informed. I hope you enjoy
Bath at Easter and when Manfred has passed his examinations he will
stay there for good. Yours ever
Dear Hannah & Manfred, I cannot tell you how
sorry I am that you misunderstood our desire to
let you participate in all our actions by giving you a complete
description of all our impressions of Eva and Salmon's, of all our
deliberations, enquiries and decisions. We did not criticize Eva for
not being a "loving daughter" to Mr. Salmon. We tried to describe you the
whole situation in greatest detail and to explain their and Eva's feelings
in order to explain why their relationship was not perfect, although they
were very nice and pleasant together. There was nothing else behind it
as you seem to imagine and Eva did not behave badly at all.
Stefan Zweig
